q: Which of the following is a method used to teach autistic children?
concept: The answer is a: the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) is a method used to teach autistic children. Andy Bondy and Lori Frost (1985) developed it at the Delaware Autistic Program for children with autism who had little or no functional speech. PECS rests on applied behaviour analysis: the child learns to hand a picture card to a communication partner in exchange for the item shown, and getting that item is the reward. It moves through six phases: (1) the physical exchange of a single picture; (2) distance and persistence (going to the partner and to the picture book); (3) discriminating between pictures; (4) building a sentence strip ('I want' plus a picture); (5) answering 'What do you want?'; and (6) commenting ('I see', 'I hear'). Because the child must approach another person, PECS teaches initiation and the social nature of communication, a core difficulty in autism, and many children go on to develop some speech. It is a form of augmentative and alternative communication (AAC). Aarav, a four-year-old autistic boy who used to scream when hungry, learns to pick up a picture of a biscuit and give it to his teacher; the request replaces the scream. Option a is right because PECS was designed specifically for autistic children with communication difficulties. Exam trap: Braille and the Taylor frame are also special education methods and appear in the same lists, but they serve children with visual impairment, not autism.

traps.b: Braille, devised by Louis Braille (1824), is a tactile reading and writing code of raised dots for people who are blind or visually impaired, not an autism intervention.
traps.c: The Taylor frame is a metal slate with star-shaped holes into which shaped pegs are set to do arithmetic; it is a mathematics aid for blind pupils, not for autism.
traps.d: PECS (option a) is a well-established method for autistic children, so 'none of these' is wrong.

q: A person with multiple distinct personalities within one body likely suffers from:
concept: Dissociative identity disorder (DID), formerly called multiple personality disorder, is a dissociative disorder in the DSM-5 characterized by the presence of two or more distinct personality states, or identities, that recurrently take control of the person's behavior, accompanied by gaps in memory (dissociative amnesia) that exceed ordinary forgetting. It is understood as a severe dissociative response, typically linked to overwhelming early childhood trauma, in which the sense of self fragments as a protective mechanism. A crucial and frequently tested distinction is that DID is not schizophrenia. Schizophrenia, whose name coined by Eugen Bleuler literally means split mind, refers to a splitting of psychic functions and a break from reality marked by hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thought, not to multiple personalities. Bipolar disorder involves episodic mood swings, and borderline personality disorder involves pervasive instability of identity, affect, and relationships without truly separate identities. Because multiple distinct personalities within one person define DID, option a is correct.

traps.b: Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder involving hallucinations and delusions; the split it involves is a split from reality, not multiple personalities, a common lay confusion.
traps.c: Bipolar disorder involves cycling mood episodes (mania and depression), not multiple identities.
traps.d: Borderline personality disorder features identity disturbance and instability, but not fully separate distinct personality states.

q: The theoretical position that says the whole is more than the sum of the parts is:
concept: The answer is b: Gestalt psychology holds that the whole is more than (strictly, different from) the sum of its parts. Gestalt is German for an organised whole or form. The school began when Max Wertheimer (1912) reported the phi phenomenon: two lines flashed about 60 milliseconds apart look like one line moving. The motion lies in neither stimulus, so no adding up of sensations can produce it. With Wolfgang Köhler (1887 to 1967) and Kurt Koffka (1886 to 1941), Wertheimer attacked structuralism, which broke consciousness into elements, and behaviourism, which broke behaviour into reflexes. Gestalt psychologists studied wholes and relations instead: figure and ground, the laws of grouping (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, Prägnanz), Köhler's insight in chimpanzees and the field theory of Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947). Koffka preferred 'different from' to 'more than', because the whole has its own properties, not just extra ones. Example: Meera hears a song played in a different key. Every note has changed, yet she recognises the melody at once, because the tune lives in the relations between notes, not in the notes themselves. Option b is right because the whole-over-parts slogan is the founding claim of Gestalt psychology. Exam trap: Wilhelm Wundt's (1832 to 1920) creative synthesis and John Stuart Mill's (1806 to 1873) mental chemistry also say a whole gains new properties, so setters sometimes bait with structuralism or associationism; but the slogan and the theoretical position belong to Gestalt.

traps.a: Cognitive psychology (the cognitive revolution from 1956; Ulric Neisser's Cognitive Psychology, 1967) studies the mind as an information processor, often breaking tasks into stages, which is close to the opposite of a holistic slogan.
traps.c: Behaviourism (John B. Watson, 1913) is elementistic: it builds behaviour out of stimulus-response links and reflexes, the very analysis Gestalt rejected.
traps.d: Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud) explains behaviour through unconscious conflict among id, ego and superego; it has no whole-and-parts principle of perception.

q: Which of the following is not one of the Big Five personality factors?
concept: The answer is c: submissiveness is not one of the Big Five personality factors. The Big Five, or Five-Factor Model, is the most widely accepted map of broad personality traits. It grew from the lexical hypothesis: the important ways people differ become words in everyday language, so factor-analysing trait words should reveal the main dimensions. Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal (1961) found five factors in US Air Force ratings, Warren Norman (1963) confirmed them, and Lewis Goldberg (1981) named them the Big Five. Paul Costa and Robert McCrae (1985) reached the same five with questionnaires and built the NEO Personality Inventory (revised as the NEO-PI-R, 1992). Remember them as OCEAN: Openness to experience (curious, imaginative), Conscientiousness (organised, dependable), Extraversion (sociable, energetic), Agreeableness (kind, cooperative) and Neuroticism (anxious and moody, as against emotionally stable). Each is a continuum, and most people score near the middle. For example, Arjun may score high on conscientiousness, never missing a deadline, but low on extraversion, preferring a quiet evening at home. Submissiveness, a tendency to yield to others and avoid confrontation, is a narrower quality. In the NEO-PI-R, assertiveness is a facet of extraversion and compliance is a facet of agreeableness, so submissiveness overlaps with pieces of two factors but is not a factor itself. Option c is right because extraversion, agreeableness and openness to experience are three of the five named factors, while submissiveness is not on the list. Exam trap: dominance versus submissiveness does appear in other trait systems, for example as factor E (dominance) in Raymond Cattell's 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire (1949), so it sounds like a standard trait; it is still not one of the Big Five.

traps.a: Extraversion (sociable, talkative, energetic versus reserved) is the E in OCEAN, so it is one of the Big Five.
traps.b: Agreeableness (trusting, kind, cooperative versus antagonistic) is the A in OCEAN, so it is one of the Big Five.
traps.d: Openness to experience (curious, imaginative, open to new ideas versus conventional) is the O in OCEAN, so it is one of the Big Five.

q: What brain structure is primarily involved in emotion processing?
concept: The amygdala is an almond-shaped cluster of nuclei located deep within the temporal lobes and is a core component of the limbic system, the brain's emotional network described by Paul MacLean. It is the structure most centrally involved in processing emotions, especially fear, threat detection, and the assignment of emotional significance to stimuli. Research by Joseph LeDoux mapped the neural pathways of fear, showing a fast subcortical route by which sensory information reaches the amygdala directly from the thalamus, allowing rapid, pre-conscious responses to danger, alongside a slower cortical route. The amygdala also modulates the strength of emotional memories via its interactions with the hippocampus, helping explain the vividness of flashbulb memories (Roger Brown and James Kulik, 1977). Damage to the amygdala can impair the recognition of fear in others and blunt fear conditioning. The distractors serve other roles: the frontal lobe handles executive control and emotion regulation, the cerebellum coordinates movement, and the brainstem governs vital autonomic functions. Because the amygdala is the structure primarily responsible for emotion processing, option c is correct.

traps.a: The frontal lobe supports executive function and emotional regulation, but the primary structure for generating and processing emotion, especially fear, is the amygdala.
traps.b: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, not emotion.
traps.d: The brainstem controls basic life functions such as breathing and heart rate, not emotion processing.

q: According to social-exchange theory we will help when:

options.a: The benefits are external and the costs are internal.
options.b: The benefits are greater than the costs.
options.c: The benefits and costs are proportional.
options.d: The benefits are smaller than the costs.

concept: The answer is b: social exchange theory predicts that we help when the benefits of helping are greater than the costs. Social exchange theory, developed by George Homans (1958) and by John Thibaut and Harold Kelley (1959), treats social life as a kind of trade in which people try, often without noticing, to maximise rewards and minimise costs. Applied to helping, a bystander weighs what helping would bring against what it would cost. Rewards can be external, such as praise, payment or a good reputation, or internal, such as relief from one's own distress at seeing someone suffer, or feeling good about oneself. Costs include time, effort, danger and embarrassment. On this view even helping that looks unselfish is partly self-interested, so the theory sides with psychological egoism in the debate about true altruism. The arousal: cost-reward model of Jane Piliavin and colleagues (1981) uses the same logic: seeing someone in distress causes unpleasant arousal, which bystanders reduce by the cheapest route, so they help when the costs of helping are low and the costs of not helping (guilt, blame) are high. In their New York subway studies (1969), a collapsed man with a cane was helped far more often than one who seemed drunk. Example: Meera stops to help an elderly man pick up his spilt fruit because it takes a minute and she feels good, but drives past a stranded car on a dark highway because the risk feels too high. Option b is right because helping occurs when perceived rewards outweigh perceived costs. Exam trap: a borrows the theory's real external and internal language but garbles it; benefits and costs can each be external or internal, and what matters is which side is larger.

q: Mongolism occurs due to:
concept: The answer is b: the condition is caused by an extra chromosome on pair 21. Humans normally have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; pairs 1 to 22 are autosomes and pair 23 is the sex chromosomes (XX or XY). The English physician John Langdon Down (1866) first described the condition, and in 1959 Jérôme Lejeune, with Marthe Gautier and Raymond Turpin, found its cause: a third copy of chromosome 21, giving 47 chromosomes in all. This is trisomy 21. "Mongolism", the word in the stem, is an old, offensive term based on a racial comparison and is no longer used; the condition is Down syndrome. About 95 percent of cases arise from nondisjunction, when the two copies of chromosome 21 fail to separate during meiosis, usually in the egg; the rest come from translocation or mosaicism. The risk rises sharply with the mother's age, especially after about 35. Typical features are intellectual disability (usually mild to moderate), a flat facial profile, upward slanting eyes, a single crease across the palm, low muscle tone, heart defects and, later in life, early Alzheimer's disease, because chromosome 21 carries the amyloid precursor protein gene. A baby girl, Anaya, born to a 41-year-old mother, may be picked up by prenatal screening and then confirmed by a karyotype showing three copies of chromosome 21. Option b is right because Down syndrome is trisomy 21, an extra autosome on pair 21. Exam trap: pair 23 is the sex chromosome pair, so an extra chromosome there gives conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), not Down syndrome; and an extra Y gives 47,XYY.

traps.a: Pair 23 is the sex chromosome pair; an extra chromosome there produces sex chromosome conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) or triple X (47,XXX), not Down syndrome.
traps.c: No classic syndrome comes from an extra chromosome 20; the well-known autosomal trisomies seen in live births are 21 (Down), 18 (Edwards) and 13 (Patau).
traps.d: An extra Y chromosome gives 47,XYY syndrome in males, usually with tall stature and few other signs; it is a sex chromosome condition, not Down syndrome.

q: A researcher uses an experimental design to study the effect of music on memory. In this experiment, the Independent Variable is:
concept: The answer is a: music is the independent variable, the factor the researcher changes to see its effect. In an experiment the researcher manipulates one variable and measures another, while holding everything else constant. The independent variable (IV) is the one the experimenter manipulates or varies; its different values are called levels or conditions (for example, music versus silence, or classical versus rock versus none). The dependent variable (DV) is the outcome that is measured, the behaviour expected to 'depend' on the IV. Here the DV is memory, measured perhaps as the number of words recalled. Anything else that could affect recall, such as time of day, list difficulty or participants' age, is an extraneous variable that must be controlled, so that any difference in memory can be credited to the music. A simple rule: the IV is the cause the researcher sets, the DV is the effect the researcher records. Stems often follow the pattern 'the effect of IV on DV', and this one reads 'the effect of music (IV) on memory (DV)'. For example, Meera gives one group of students a word list to learn while Indian classical music plays and another group the same list in silence, then counts how many words each student recalls. She decided who heard music, so music is the IV; the recall scores are the DV. Option a is right because music is what the researcher manipulates, and memory is what is measured as the result. Exam trap: examiners reverse the pair and offer the DV (memory) as the IV. Another trick is 'both', which forgets that one variable cannot be both the manipulated cause and the measured outcome in the same experiment. Note too that a purely correlational study has no true IV, because nothing is manipulated.

traps.b: Memory is the dependent variable, the outcome the researcher measures (for example words recalled) to see whether the music changed it.
traps.c: An experiment separates the manipulated cause from the measured effect; music and memory play different roles, so they cannot both be the IV.
traps.d: This would fit only if nothing were manipulated; here music is deliberately varied (IV) and memory is measured (DV).

q: MMPI is a test of:
concept: The answer is c: the MMPI is a test of personality, and in particular of psychopathology. The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory was published by the psychologist Starke Hathaway and the psychiatrist J. Charnley McKinley (1943) at the University of Minnesota. It is an objective, self-report inventory: the person marks hundreds of statements as true or false, and the answers are scored against fixed norms rather than interpreted freely. Its items were chosen by empirical criterion keying. An item stayed on a scale only if patients with a given diagnosis (for example, depression) answered it differently from ordinary people, whatever the item seemed to be about. The result is 10 clinical scales, such as Hypochondriasis, Depression, Hysteria, Psychopathic Deviate, Paranoia and Schizophrenia, plus validity scales (L for lying, F for rare or infrequent answers, K for defensiveness) that show whether the person answered honestly. The MMPI-2 (1989) has 567 items and is still among the most used personality tests in clinics. For example, when Kabir is referred for low mood and unexplained bodily complaints, his MMPI-2 profile can show raised Depression and Hypochondriasis scales, and the validity scales tell the clinician whether he was faking good or faking bad. Option c is right because the MMPI describes personality traits and clinical patterns, not ability, opinions or vocational likes. Exam trap: the word 'multiphasic' makes some students think of a multi-ability battery; it only means many scales of personality. Also, the MMPI is an objective test, so do not group it with projective tests such as the Rorschach or the TAT.

traps.a: Intelligence is measured by ability tests such as David Wechsler's WAIS or the Stanford-Binet, which have right and wrong answers; the MMPI has no right answers.
traps.b: Attitudes are measured by scales such as Louis Thurstone's (1928) equal-appearing intervals or Rensis Likert's (1932) agree-disagree scale, which ask for opinions on a topic, not personality traits.
traps.d: Interest is measured by inventories such as Edward Strong's Strong Vocational Interest Blank (1927) or the Kuder Preference Record, which compare a person's likes with those of people in different jobs.

q: Assertion (A): The ethical principle of confidentiality is crucial in counseling and prohibits counselors from sharing client information without consent. Reason (R): Maintaining confidentiality helps to establish trust and encourages clients to open up about sensitive issues.

options.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is true, but R is false
options.d: A is false, but R is true

concept: The answer is a: both statements are true, and R correctly explains A. Statement A is true. Confidentiality is the counsellor's ethical duty not to reveal what a client discloses, or even that the person is a client, without the client's informed consent. Every major code puts it at the centre: the American Psychological Association's Ethics Code (2002) gives it a whole section, and India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017 gives people with mental illness a right to confidentiality. It is not absolute. Disclosure is allowed or required when there is serious risk of suicide or of harm to an identifiable person (the duty to protect that followed Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California, 1976), when child abuse is suspected (India's POCSO Act 2012 makes reporting sexual offences against children mandatory) and under a court order. Clients should hear these limits in the first session, as part of informed consent. With those limits understood, A states the rule accurately. Statement R is also true. Clients talk about shame, sexuality, abuse, addiction and suicidal thoughts only if they trust that the information will not reach their family, employer or community. Does R explain A? Yes: confidentiality is crucial precisely because counselling works only when clients feel safe enough to disclose. Example: Kabir, a college student, tells his counsellor about his gambling debts only after she explains that nothing will be shared with his parents unless he is at risk of harming himself or someone else. Option a is right because both statements are accurate and R gives the reason the rule matters. Exam trap: candidates who know the exceptions sometimes call A false, but limits to confidentiality do not cancel the principle; they only define when it gives way.

traps.b: This verdict needs an R that is true but beside the point; here R gives the very reason confidentiality is crucial, trust and open disclosure, so it explains A.
traps.c: R is not false: the link between confidentiality, trust and disclosure is the standard rationale given in counselling and psychology ethics codes.
traps.d: A is not false: the legal and ethical exceptions (risk of harm, child abuse, court orders) limit the rule but do not cancel it, so the principle as stated is accurate.

q: X-linked recessive conditions associated with mental retardation include all the following, EXCEPT:
concept: The answer is d: cri-du-chat syndrome is not an X-linked recessive condition; it is an autosomal chromosomal deletion. In X-linked recessive inheritance the faulty gene lies on the X chromosome. A female with one faulty copy is usually a healthy carrier, because her second X masks it; a male has only one X, so a single faulty copy produces the disorder. Such conditions therefore strike mainly boys and pass through carrier mothers. If Meera carries a faulty X-linked gene, each son has a 50% chance of being affected and each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier. Three of the options follow this pattern and can impair intellect. Duchenne muscular dystrophy comes from mutations in the dystrophin gene on the X; boys develop progressive muscle weakness, and about a third also have cognitive impairment. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, described by Michael Lesch and William Nyhan (1964), is a deficiency of the enzyme HPRT, causing excess uric acid, dystonia, intellectual disability and striking self-biting. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy comes from ABCD1 mutations; very long chain fatty acids build up, and the childhood cerebral form brings behavioural and cognitive decline as myelin breaks down. Cri-du-chat syndrome, identified by Jerome Lejeune (1963), is a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p minus), so it affects both sexes; infants have a high, cat-like cry, a small head and severe intellectual disability. Option d is right because its cause lies on an autosome, not on the X. Exam trap: 'genetic' is not the same as 'X-linked'; deletion syndromes (cri-du-chat, Williams, Prader-Willi) are chromosomal errors, whereas fragile X, Lesch-Nyhan and Duchenne sit on the X.

q: Latent learning challenges which of the following assumptions of strict behaviorism?

options.b: Reinforcement is required for learning to occur
options.c: Extinction reduces the likelihood of behavior permanently

concept: The answer is b: latent learning challenges the strict behaviourist assumption that reinforcement is required for learning to occur. For behaviourists such as Edward Thorndike and Clark Hull, learning meant stamping in stimulus-response connections through reward: no reinforcement, no learning. Edward Chace Tolman (1886 to 1959), a purposive behaviourist at Berkeley, disagreed. In Tolman and Charles Honzik's experiment (1930), three groups of hungry rats ran a complex maze daily. One group always found food in the goal box, one never did, and the third found food only from day 11. Until then the third group made as many errors as the never-rewarded rats, but once food appeared its errors fell almost at once to the level of the always-rewarded group. It must have been learning the maze all along without reward; the food only gave it a reason to show what it knew. This is latent learning: learning without obvious reinforcement that stays hidden until there is an incentive to perform. Tolman (1948) said the rats had built a cognitive map, a mental representation of the maze. The study separates learning from performance, a distinction Albert Bandura later drew on. Example: a child who rides to school in the car every day without paying attention can suddenly guide a lost visitor there; the route was learned without any reward. Option b is right because the rats learned without reinforcement, contradicting the claim that reinforcement is necessary for learning. Exam trap: latent learning and cognitive maps are Tolman's, not Kohler's (insight) or Bandura's (observational learning), although all three challenged strict behaviourism.

traps.c: Whether extinction is permanent is answered by spontaneous recovery (Pavlov), not by latent learning; behaviourists themselves accept that extinguished responses can return.
traps.d: The order of classical and operant conditioning is not an assumption of behaviourism and has nothing to do with Tolman's maze studies.

q: Self-Efficacy is

options.a: A person's mental model of his or her ability and attitudes.
options.b: A generalised evaluative attitude toward the self that influences both moods and behaviour
options.c: The process by which a person comes to know or perceive the personal attributes
options.d: A set of beliefs that one can perform adequately in a particular situation.

concept: The answer is d: self-efficacy is a set of beliefs that one can perform adequately in a particular situation. Albert Bandura (1977) introduced the idea in the Psychological Review paper 'Self-efficacy: toward a unifying theory of behavioral change', as part of what became his social cognitive theory. Self-efficacy is not a general opinion of oneself; it is a task-specific expectation: 'Can I do this, here?' A student may have high self-efficacy for mathematics and low self-efficacy for public speaking. Bandura separated efficacy expectations (I can carry out the behaviour) from outcome expectations (the behaviour will bring the result). He named four sources of efficacy beliefs: mastery experiences (past successes, the strongest source), vicarious experience (seeing similar others succeed), verbal persuasion (encouragement) and physiological and emotional states (reading a racing heart as a sign of unreadiness). High self-efficacy predicts more effort, persistence after failure and better progress in therapy, and it is a key ingredient in health behaviour change. For example, Arjun is sure he will pass his driving test because he has driven safely with his father for months, yet he doubts he could cook a meal for ten guests; his self-efficacy differs by task. Option d is right because it captures both features of Bandura's definition: a belief about one's capability, tied to a particular situation. Exam trap: option b describes self-esteem, a global evaluation of one's worth, which is often confused with self-efficacy; a person can have high self-esteem yet low self-efficacy for a specific task.

traps.b: A generalised evaluative attitude toward the self that colours mood and behaviour is self-esteem (measured, for example, by Morris Rosenberg's 1965 scale); it is global, not task-specific.
traps.c: The process of coming to know one's own attributes describes self-perception or self-knowledge, as in Daryl Bem's (1967) self-perception theory, where we infer our attitudes from our own behaviour.

q: During the propagation of an action potential, which event ensures the unidirectional flow of the neural impulse along the axon?

options.a: The absolute refractory period caused by voltage-gated sodium channel inactivation.
options.b: The relative refractory period caused by the hyperpolarization of the membrane.
options.c: The saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons.
options.d: The temporal summation of excitatory postsynaptic potentials at the axon hillock.

concept: The answer is a: the absolute refractory period, caused by inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, ensures that an action potential travels only one way along the axon. Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley (1952) worked out the ionic basis of the action potential from the squid giant axon. When the membrane at one point reaches threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and sodium rushes in, driving the inside positive. Within about a millisecond these channels inactivate: an inactivation gate plugs them, and they cannot reopen until the membrane has repolarised. For roughly 1 to 2 milliseconds after a spike begins, no stimulus, however strong, can fire that patch again. This is the absolute refractory period. Now follow the impulse. Current from the active patch spreads passively in both directions. Ahead lies resting membrane, which is pushed to threshold and fires. Behind lies the patch that has just fired, whose Na+ channels are still inactivated, so the spreading current cannot trigger it. The spike therefore moves forward only, from axon hillock to terminal buttons, like a flame along a Diwali fuse that cannot burn back over the part already burnt. The same period also limits how fast a neuron can fire. If an axon is stimulated artificially in the middle, spikes run in both directions, which shows that direction depends on where firing starts and on refractoriness, not on any one-way property of the axon itself. Option a is right because sodium channel inactivation makes the membrane just behind the spike temporarily unexcitable. Exam trap: the relative refractory period also follows the spike, so option b tempts; but during it a strong enough stimulus can still fire the membrane, so it cannot guarantee one-way travel, and it reflects open potassium channels rather than inactivated sodium channels.

traps.b: The relative refractory period, when K+ channels are still open and the membrane is hyperpolarised, only raises the threshold; a strong stimulus can still fire, so it limits firing frequency rather than fixing direction.
traps.c: Saltatory conduction, the node-to-node jumping of the impulse in myelinated axons, increases speed; its direction is still set by the refractory node just behind, and unmyelinated axons conduct one way too.
traps.d: Temporal summation of EPSPs at the axon hillock decides whether an action potential starts, by adding inputs over time; it says nothing about which way the spike travels once it has begun.

q: According to Harold Kelley's Covariation Model of attribution, an observer will make an external attribution when a target's behavior exhibits :

options.a: Low distinctiveness, low consensus, and high consistency
options.b: High distinctiveness, low consensus, and low consistency
options.c: Low distinctiveness, high consensus, and low consistency
options.d: High distinctiveness, high consensus, and high consistency

concept: The answer is d: Harold Kelley's covariation model predicts an external attribution when consensus, distinctiveness and consistency are all high. Harold Kelley (1967) asked how we decide whether a behaviour is caused by the person, the stimulus or the circumstances. His answer is that we act like intuitive scientists: across many observations we credit the cause that varies together, or covaries, with the behaviour. Three kinds of information matter. Consensus asks whether other people react to the same stimulus in the same way. Distinctiveness asks whether this person reacts differently to other stimuli. Consistency asks whether this person reacts the same way to this stimulus on other occasions. High consensus, high distinctiveness and high consistency point outward, to the stimulus or situation. Low consensus, low distinctiveness and high consistency point inward, to the person's disposition. Low consistency points to passing circumstances. Leslie McArthur (1972) tested the model with written vignettes and found that people do use all three cues, though they underuse consensus. Example: Kabir laughs at a stand-up comedian. Everyone else in the hall laughs too (high consensus), Kabir rarely laughs at other comedians (high distinctiveness) and he laughs at this one every time (high consistency). We conclude the comedian is genuinely funny: an external cause. Option d is right because only the all-high pattern points to the stimulus. Exam trap: option a is the mirror image, the classic pattern for an internal attribution; consistency is high in both patterns, and examiners rely on students forgetting that consensus and distinctiveness flip.

traps.a: Low distinctiveness, low consensus and high consistency is Harold Kelley's pattern for an internal (dispositional) attribution: the person reacts this way to everything, nobody else does, and it happens every time.
traps.b: High distinctiveness and low consensus with low consistency leads to a circumstance attribution in Harold Kelley's model; low consistency marks the behaviour as a one-off, put down to passing conditions rather than the stimulus.
traps.c: Low distinctiveness, high consensus and low consistency is a mixed, ambiguous pattern; with low consistency the observer again leans towards a circumstantial explanation, not a clear external attribution to the stimulus.

q: Piaget believed that object permanence is typically attained during which stage?
concept: The answer is d: Piaget believed object permanence is attained in the sensorimotor stage, from birth to about 2 years. Jean Piaget (1936, 1954) described four stages of cognitive development: sensorimotor (birth to 2), preoperational (2 to 7), concrete operational (7 to 11) and formal operational (11 or 12 onwards). Object permanence is the understanding that objects go on existing when they cannot be seen, heard or touched. Piaget tested it by hiding a toy under a cloth while the infant watched. Before about 8 months, an infant who sees a toy covered acts as if it has vanished ('out of sight, out of mind'). In substage 4 (8 to 12 months) the infant searches for a fully hidden object but makes the A-not-B error: after finding the toy under cloth A several times, she keeps searching at A even after watching it being moved to B. By substage 6 (18 to 24 months), with mental representation, she can follow invisible moves and the concept is complete. Later work, notably Renée Baillargeon's (1987) looking-time studies, found signs of object permanence as early as 3 to 4 months, suggesting Piaget underestimated infants; but the stage he placed it in is still the sensorimotor. For example, at 6 months baby Arjun stops reaching when his rattle is covered with a towel; at 10 months he pulls the towel off to get it. Option d is right because object permanence is the major achievement of Piaget's sensorimotor period. Exam trap: examiners offer preoperational because object permanence is completed near age 2, the boundary. Conservation, not object permanence, is the hallmark of the concrete operational stage, and abstract hypothetical thinking marks formal operations.

traps.a: Formal operations (11 or 12 years onwards) is the stage of abstract, hypothetical and propositional reasoning; object permanence was achieved about a decade earlier.
traps.b: Concrete operations (7 to 11 years) is marked by conservation, reversibility and classification, not object permanence.
traps.c: The preoperational stage (2 to 7) begins with object permanence already in place; it is marked by symbolic play, egocentrism and lack of conservation.

q: The probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis is known as:
concept: The answer is a: the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis is the probability of a Type I error, written alpha. In significance testing the null hypothesis (H0) states that there is no effect or difference. Because decisions are made from samples, two mistakes are possible. A Type I error (alpha error) is rejecting H0 when it is actually true: a false positive. A Type II error (beta error) is retaining H0 when it is actually false: a false negative, a real effect missed. Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson, in papers of 1928 and 1933, framed testing as a decision between H0 and an alternative hypothesis with fixed error rates, which gave us these two errors and the idea of power (1 minus beta). The researcher chooses alpha in advance, usually .05 or .01, so the significance level is the Type I error rate. With sample size fixed, lowering alpha cuts Type I errors but raises beta; only a larger sample or a more precise measure reduces both. Example: a trial concludes at p < .05 that a new antidepressant beats placebo, but in truth the drug has no effect; the researchers have made a Type I error. In court terms, a Type I error convicts the innocent and a Type II error frees the guilty. Option a is right because rejecting a true null is the textbook definition of a Type I error. Exam trap: examiners swap the wordings; accepting a false null is Type II, and the probability of correctly rejecting a false null is power, not alpha.

traps.b: A Type II error is failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false, missing a real effect; its probability is beta, the opposite mistake from the one in the stem.
traps.c: A confidence interval is a range of values that, with a stated confidence such as 95 percent, is expected to contain the population parameter; it is an estimate, not an error probability.
traps.d: The standard deviation is a descriptive measure of how spread out scores are around the mean; it has nothing to do with decision errors in hypothesis testing.

q: A newly constructed test of creativity has a +0.15 correlation with four other standardised creativity scales and a correlation of +1.00 between the scores of any student who takes the test twice. This indicates that the test has:

options.a: High content validity but low reliability
options.b: Moderate external validity and moderate reliability
options.c: Low face validity but high reliability
options.d: Low criterion validity but high reliability

concept: The answer is d: the test has low criterion validity but high reliability. Reliability is consistency: does the test give the same result each time? A test-retest correlation of +1.00 means every student got the same score both times, which is perfect reliability (stability). Validity is accuracy: does the test measure what it claims to measure? One way to check is criterion-related validity, correlating the new test with an outside standard. When the standard is a set of established tests of the same trait given at about the same time, the result is concurrent validity, and in the multitrait-multimethod terms of Donald Campbell and Donald Fiske (1959) it is also evidence of convergent validity. Here the new test correlates only +0.15 with four standard creativity scales, so it shares very little with them: whatever it measures so consistently, it is probably not creativity as those scales define it. Option d is right because a near-zero correlation with accepted criterion measures means low criterion validity, while the perfect retest correlation means high reliability. The case shows the classic rule that reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A bathroom scale that always reads 5 kg too light is perfectly reliable but not valid. Exam trap: students see 'high reliability' and jump to option c, but face validity is judged simply by looking at the items (does it look like a creativity test to those who take it?), so no correlation can show it is low. The same holds for content validity in option a, which experts judge by inspecting how well the items cover the domain; and a's 'low reliability' is wrong in any case.

traps.b: A correlation of +0.15 is weak, not moderate, evidence of validity against outside measures, and +1.00 is perfect, not moderate, reliability; 'external validity' is in any case a research design term for how far results generalise.
traps.c: The reliability half is right, but face validity is whether the test looks suitable to the people taking it; it is judged by inspection, so these correlations say nothing about it.

q: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) was originally developed for treating which disorder?
concept: The answer is c: dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) was originally developed for treating borderline personality disorder. Marsha Linehan, an American psychologist at the University of Washington, developed it for chronically suicidal, self-harming women, most of whom met criteria for borderline personality disorder (BPD), and published the treatment manuals in 1993. Standard CBT's constant push for change felt invalidating to these clients and many dropped out, yet acceptance alone did not stop the self-harm. DBT's dialectic synthesises the two: full acceptance of the person together with a firm push for change. The acceptance side, including mindfulness, came from Zen practice; the change side came from behaviour therapy. Linehan's biosocial theory sees BPD as pervasive emotion dysregulation that arises when a biologically sensitive, reactive child grows up in an invalidating environment. q: People with ______ avoid specific public places or situations because they anticipate having anxiety or a panic attack and being unable to escape or get help.
concept: The answer is b: this describes agoraphobia. The word comes from the Greek agora, the marketplace, so it literally means fear of the marketplace or of public places. In DSM-5 (2013), agoraphobia is marked fear or anxiety about at least two of five kinds of situation: using public transport, being in open spaces such as car parks or bridges, being in enclosed places such as shops or cinemas, standing in a queue or a crowd, and being outside the home alone. The core of the fear is not the place itself but the thought that escape might be difficult, or help unavailable, if panic-like or embarrassing symptoms struck. The situations are avoided, endured with intense dread or faced only with a companion, and the problem typically lasts 6 months or more. Since DSM-5 it is diagnosed separately from panic disorder, though the two often occur together and a person can receive both. Alan Goldstein and Dianne Chambless (1978) described the mechanism as "fear of fear": after a few panic attacks, people come to dread the bodily sensations themselves and the places where attacks happened. Picture Riya, who had a panic attack on a crowded Delhi Metro train: she now travels only by autorickshaw, avoids malls and will not go to the market without her sister. Option b is right because the stem describes avoiding public places for fear of being unable to escape or get help during panic. Exam trap: social phobia also leads to avoidance of public situations, but there the feared outcome is being judged or embarrassed by others, not being trapped without help.

traps.a: Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) is fear of situations in which one may be watched and negatively evaluated, such as speaking or eating in public; the feared outcome is humiliation, not being unable to escape during panic.
traps.c: 'Panic xenophobia' is not a diagnosis; xenophobia means fear or dislike of strangers or foreigners, a social attitude rather than an anxiety disorder, attached to 'panic' to sound plausible.
traps.d: Acrophobia is a specific phobia of heights; the fear is tied to one kind of stimulus, not to a range of public places from which escape might be hard.

q: Our current mood and feelings are best described by the term:
concept: The correct answer is affect. In psychiatric and psychological terminology, careful distinctions are drawn among affect, mood, emotion, and feeling. Affect refers to the immediate, observable, and momentary expression of emotion, the current emotional state as it is displayed and experienced in the present moment; it is what a clinician observes and rates during a mental status examination (for example, describing affect as flat, blunted, restricted, labile, or congruent with mood). Because the question asks about our current mood and feelings in the immediate sense, affect is the best fit, as it denotes the present, here-and-now emotional state. Mood, by contrast, is the more sustained, pervasive, and prolonged emotional climate, the emotional background that colours a person's experience over a longer period (days or weeks), often compared to the climate, whereas affect is like the weather of a particular moment. Emotion is a broader term for a complex reaction involving physiological arousal, subjective experience, cognitive appraisal, and behavioural expression in response to a stimulus. Feeling is the subjective, conscious experience of an emotion. In clinical usage, affect is the cross-sectional, momentary emotional expression, which is why it is the answer for the current emotional state.

traps.a: Emotion is a broad, complex reaction (arousal plus appraisal plus expression) rather than specifically the current, momentary emotional state being asked about.
traps.b: Mood is the sustained, pervasive emotional climate over time, not the immediate present-moment state that affect denotes.
traps.d: Feeling is the subjective conscious experience of emotion, a narrower internal sense, not the observed current emotional expression that defines affect.

q: Deepika is unable to gain threatening or anxiety-provoking material into her access to conscious awareness. This phenomenon occurs due to____________________.
concept: The correct answer is repression. Repression is the cornerstone defence mechanism of Freudian psychoanalysis, described by Freud as the basic mechanism on which all others rest. It is the unconscious, automatic exclusion of threatening, anxiety-provoking, or unacceptable thoughts, memories, impulses, and feelings from conscious awareness, pushing them down into the unconscious where they cannot be voluntarily retrieved. In this example, Deepika is unable to bring anxiety-provoking material into conscious awareness, which is precisely repression: the material is actively (though unconsciously) kept out of consciousness. The critical distinction Sihan must master is between repression and suppression. Repression is unconscious and involuntary; the person is not aware they are doing it and cannot simply choose to recall the material. Suppression, by contrast, is conscious and deliberate; the person knowingly and intentionally pushes a thought aside, choosing not to dwell on it for now, with the ability to bring it back later. Because the question describes an inability to gain access to the material (an involuntary blocking) rather than a deliberate choice to set it aside, the mechanism is repression. Freud believed repressed material does not vanish but continues to exert influence, leaking out in dreams, slips of the tongue, and neurotic symptoms.

traps.a: Suppression is the conscious, deliberate setting aside of a thought that one can later recall; the question describes involuntary inability to access, which is repression.
traps.c: Depression is a mood disorder, not a defence mechanism, and does not describe the blocking of material from awareness.
traps.d: Denial refuses to acknowledge an external reality; here the issue is the unconscious blocking of internal anxiety-provoking material, which is repression.

q: Match List I (Neurological condition) with List II (Brain site): A. Finger agnosia, B. Dressing apraxia, C. General amnesic syndrome, D. Intermanual conflict. 1. Bilateral medial temporal lesions, 2. Right posterior parieto-temporal area, 3. Left posterior brain, 4. Cerebral commissurotomy
concept: The answer is b: A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4. Finger agnosia (A) is the inability to name, point to or tell apart one's own or another person's fingers. It follows damage to the left posterior brain, at the angular gyrus of the parietal lobe, Josef Gerstmann (1924) first described it, and it became the core of his syndrome with agraphia, acalculia and left-right confusion: so A-3. Dressing apraxia (B) is difficulty putting on clothes, with sleeves, buttons and the left and right sides muddled, from a breakdown of spatial and body-schema processing. It goes with right posterior parieto-temporal damage, often alongside left-sided neglect and constructional apraxia: so B-2. The general amnesic syndrome (C), a dense anterograde amnesia with intact intelligence and short-term memory, follows bilateral medial temporal lesions of the hippocampus and nearby cortex, as in the patient H.M. after William Scoville's (1953) operation, studied by Brenda Milner (1957): so C-1. Intermanual conflict (D), in which one hand undoes what the other does (one buttons a shirt while the other unbuttons it), is a callosal sign after cerebral commissurotomy, the split-brain operation studied by Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga (1960s), and is a form of alien hand behaviour: so D-4. When Ramesh, after a right parietal stroke, puts his shirt on inside out and cannot find the left sleeve, that is dressing apraxia. Option b is right because it gives exactly these four pairs. Exam trap: the two parietal syndromes are easily swapped, so remember that finger agnosia is left (with the language-linked Gerstmann signs) and dressing apraxia is right (with spatial neglect); option a makes exactly that swap.

traps.a: This swaps A and B: finger agnosia is the left posterior (Gerstmann) sign and dressing apraxia the right parieto-temporal one, not the reverse.
traps.c: A-3 is right, but dressing apraxia is not a split-brain sign, amnesia does not come from the right parieto-temporal area, and intermanual conflict is not a medial temporal lesion effect.
traps.d: A-3 and C-1 are right, but it gives dressing apraxia to commissurotomy and intermanual conflict to the right parieto-temporal area, reversing the true B and D sites.

q: The bystander effect can best be explained by:
concept: The answer is a: the bystander effect is best explained by diffusion of responsibility, the sense that when many people are present, each one is less personally responsible for helping. The bystander effect is the finding that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help, and the slower help comes. It was prompted by the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York, where newspapers reported that 38 neighbours watched and none called the police (a figure later shown to be exaggerated). John Darley and Bibb Latané (1968) staged an emergency: students talking over an intercom heard another participant apparently having a seizure. When students believed they were the only listener, about 85 per cent went to help before the seizure ended; when they believed four others could also hear, only about 31 per cent did. Each person assumed someone else would act. Their later decision model (The Unresponsive Bystander, 1970) lists five steps: notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, assume responsibility, know how to help, and decide to help. Diffusion of responsibility blocks the third step; pluralistic ignorance, where everyone looks calm so no one reads the event as an emergency, blocks the second. Example: on a crowded Mumbai platform a man collapses; Meera sees dozens of people nearby and assumes one of them, perhaps a doctor, will help, so she walks on. Option a is right because spreading responsibility across many witnesses is the core explanation Darley and Latané gave. Exam trap: social loafing (c) also involves responsibility spread across a group, but it is reduced effort on a shared task, not failure to help in an emergency.

traps.b: Increased empathy raises helping, as in C. Daniel Batson's (1991) empathy-altruism hypothesis; it cannot explain why more witnesses lead to less help.
traps.c: Social loafing (Bibb Latané and colleagues, 1979) is people putting in less effort on a group task when individual output cannot be identified; it resembles the bystander effect but concerns effort, not emergency helping.
traps.d: Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) is the discomfort of inconsistent beliefs or actions; it might explain justifying a failure to help afterwards, but not the drop in helping as the crowd grows.

q: Kohlberg is known for his theory of:
concept: The answer is d: Lawrence Kohlberg is known for his theory of moral development. Lawrence Kohlberg (1958), in his doctoral work at the University of Chicago, extended Jean Piaget's (1932) ideas on children's moral judgement into a stage theory of moral reasoning. He posed moral dilemmas, the best known being the Heinz dilemma (should a man steal an overpriced drug to save his dying wife?), and scored the reasons people gave, not their yes or no answers. He described three levels with two stages each. At the preconventional level, right is what avoids punishment (Stage 1) or serves one's own interest (Stage 2). At the conventional level, right is what wins approval (Stage 3, good boy-nice girl) or upholds law and order (Stage 4). At the postconventional level, right rests on social contract and individual rights (Stage 5) and on universal ethical principles (Stage 6). The stages are said to follow an invariant order and to depend on cognitive growth. Example: asked about Heinz, Arjun (8) says he should not steal or he will go to jail (Stage 1), while his sister Riya (16) says he should steal because a good husband looks after his wife (Stage 3). Carol Gilligan (1982) criticised the theory as biased towards a male ethic of justice and proposed an ethic of care. Option d is right because Kohlberg's stages describe how moral reasoning develops. Exam trap: because Kohlberg was a cognitive-developmental theorist who built on Piaget, cognitive development (a) is the near miss; but the cognitive stages (sensorimotor to formal operations) are Piaget's, and Kohlberg's own theory is about morality.

traps.b: Social or psychosocial development is linked with Erik Erikson's eight stages (1950) and Lev Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, not with Kohlberg.
traps.c: Physical and motor development is the field of maturation theorists such as Arnold Gesell (age norms of growth), not of Kohlberg's moral dilemmas.
